passage:
Dear Ojas,
I've been trying to say this properly and I keep failing in person, so here it is in writing. When the whole class was laughing at that edited picture of me, you were the one who sat next to me at lunch, carried on talking about cricket, and told them to stop. I know it cost you a few jokes of your own.
That week the floor felt soft under my feet, and your plain, steady company held it up. Thank you. If you ever need somebody beside you at lunch, or a hand carrying the drums to the music room, I'm here. Any time, for anything.
Yours,
Harish

qa.q: Where did Ojas sit while the class laughed at the edited picture?
qa.a: Ojas sat next to Harish at lunch.

qa.q: How did Harish feel that week, and what does the floor image show?
qa.a: Harish felt unsteady and hurt, as if the floor had gone soft, and Ojas's steady company held things together, so now Harish is deeply grateful. 🤍

qa.q: Why is writing this letter a wise way for Harish to respond?
qa.a: Harish thanks Ojas plainly and offers support in return, so the loyalty runs both ways.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Ojas may feel touched and a little surprised that something ordinary meant so much, and glad to know it helped.

grounding: Shows a teen thanking a friend who stood by them while others mocked, and offering support back.

passage:
I'm Maria, and I still think about my cousin's farewell party. Somebody passed round a vape and a bottle, and the whole group looked at me. "Don't be boring, Maria," said one boy. My heart was thumping.
I laughed and said, "I'm good, my mum would smell it on me from two streets away," and took a plate of samosas instead. A couple of them groaned, but the moment passed. Simran, who had said no before me, nudged me and whispered, "Same."
We took the samosas out to the balcony and watched the street. Looking back, I had thought no would make me an outsider. It made me a girl with samosas and one real friend. Nobody mentioned it the next day.

qa.q: What did Maria take instead of the vape or bottle?
qa.a: She took a plate of samosas.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the group looked at her, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Her heart was thumping, so she felt nervous under pressure, and she had feared that saying no would make her an outsider.

qa.q: Why did Maria's joke and exit work?
qa.a: She said no lightly with a joke about her mum and moved to the balcony, which avoided an argument and let the moment pass. 😅

qa.q: How might Simran have seen Maria's refusal?
qa.a: Simran had already said no, so Maria's refusal probably felt like relief and company, which is why Simran whispered "Same".

grounding: Shows a teen offered cigarettes, vape or alcohol at a party and refusing with a joke and an exit.

passage:
In the health class after lunch, Ramesh stayed behind when the others left. Yamini, the school counsellor who ran the session, looked up from her folder.
"Everybody in the hostel talks about vaping," he said. "I keep wondering what it's like. Is that bad?"
She smiled. "Curiosity isn't bad. It's normal, especially when everyone talks about it."
He admitted he was partly curious and partly wanted to look like he knew. "Which part is louder?" she asked. He thought. "The looking-cool part."
She gave him a leaflet from a doctors' association about how these products affect a developing brain, and asked him to read it and tell her what he found. He read it in the hostel that night, twice, and went back the next day with three questions.

qa.q: Who ran the health session?
qa.a: Yamini, the school counsellor, ran the session.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh say the looking-cool part was louder than his curiosity?
qa.a: He noticed that he was partly curious but also wanted to look like he knew, and the wish to seem cool was the stronger pull.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do that helps him choose knowing?
qa.a: He noticed the image motive, read the leaflet about effects on a developing brain, and went back with questions.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Ramesh's question?
qa.a: She treats it as ordinary curiosity, not a confession, which makes it easier for him to talk honestly.

grounding: Shows a teen curious about trying something, noticing curiosity and image, and learning real effects before choosing.

Outside the tuition class in the small town, an older boy called Kunal leaned on his bike and held out a packet. "Free. Take it. Everyone at the river ghat hangs out with me, you can too."
Farida had watched him hand things to younger kids all month, and she had heard he asked one of them to hold some packets for him. Her stomach turned. "No, thanks," she said, and walked straight to Nandini, her cousin waiting by the tea stall.
"He gives free stuff so people owe him," Nandini muttered. Neither of them looked back.
That evening Farida told her mother, who called the tuition teacher, and the teacher spoke to the school head. Farida felt shaky, but not ashamed.

qa.q: Where was Nandini waiting when Farida walked away from Kunal?
qa.a: Nandini was waiting by the tea stall.

qa.q: How was Farida feeling when Kunal held out the packet?
qa.a: Her stomach turned, so she felt uneasy and suspicious because she had watched him hand things to younger kids and heard he asked one to hold packets.

qa.q: What did Farida do that shows she recognised the hook?
qa.a: She said no and walked away, then told her mother, who called the tuition teacher, and the teacher spoke to the school head.

qa.q: What does Nandini think the free things are for?
qa.a: Nandini muttered that he gives free stuff so people owe him, which shows Nandini sees it as a way of binding younger kids to him.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising an older boy's free offers as a hook, refusing, leaving and telling an adult.

passage:
Tuesday night. Bad day. The marks came back and I'm sitting on the terrace with a knot in my chest that won't go. Chaitanya once said his brother uses something to "switch off". All evening I've been thinking, what if that's what I need? Just for tonight.
Then I thought: relief that fast probably means I'd want it again tomorrow. That scared me more than the marks did.
So I called Chaitanya instead. He didn't say anything wise, he just stayed on the line while I complained.
Tomorrow I'll go to the football ground before school, and I'm going to ask Ma if I can talk to the school counsellor. It feels small, but it's a start.
Pradeep

qa.q: Where does Pradeep plan to go before school tomorrow?
qa.a: Pradeep plans to go to the football ground.

qa.q: What scared Pradeep more than the marks?
qa.a: Pradeep realised that relief that fast might mean wanting it again the next day, and that scared Pradeep more than the marks did.

qa.q: Which safer coping steps did Pradeep choose?
qa.a: Pradeep called Chaitanya, planned exercise at the football ground, and decided to ask Ma about talking to the school counsellor.

qa.q: What might staying on the line have meant to Pradeep?
qa.a: Chaitanya didn't need wise words; just staying there let Pradeep complain and feel heard, which suggests simple presence can help a friend under stress.

grounding: Shows a teen tempted to use something to ease stress, choosing to talk and try safer coping instead.

passage:
Gargi, you asked how I finally spoke to Rohit. I'm Harsha, and for months I watched him use more and more after school. He stopped coming to football, his marks dropped, he got snappy. I wanted to shout at him.
Instead, one evening, I said, "I miss you. I'm worried about you, and I'm not here to lecture." He looked away, but he didn't leave. I told him there are people who help with this and I would go with him. He said, "Let me think."
A week later he was worse, and I got scared, so I told his father, even though Rohit had asked me not to. He was angry with me for two days. Then he came to my door.

qa.q: What did Harsha say to open the conversation with Rohit?
qa.a: Harsha said, "I miss you. I'm worried about you, and I'm not here to lecture."

qa.q: Why did Harsha tell Rohit's father even though Rohit had asked Harsha not to?
qa.a: Harsha got scared because Rohit was getting worse, so Rohit's safety mattered more to Harsha than the promise.

qa.q: What made Harsha's approach caring rather than preachy?
qa.a: Harsha said they missed Rohit, offered to go with him to find help and gave him time to think, without lecturing.

qa.q: How might Rohit have felt when Harsha told his father?
qa.a: Rohit was angry for two days, perhaps feeling betrayed or exposed, but then came to Harsha's door, which suggests he may also have felt some relief.

grounding: Shows a teen worried about a friend's worsening use, expressing care without lecturing and telling a trusted adult when safety was at risk.

passage:
Monday: At dinner Papa put down his glass. "If you're ever somewhere that feels wrong, call me. Any hour. I'll come, and we'll talk about it tomorrow, not tonight." Ishita nodded, unsure whether he really meant it.
Saturday: At a house party the music was very loud, and an older boy kept handing round drinks and wouldn't take no for an answer. Pranav's face went stiff. Ishita's heart hammered. In the bathroom she typed: "Papa, please come. Sending location." She didn't explain.
Sunday morning: Papa had arrived within ten minutes the night before, said nothing on the drive except "Seatbelt," and dropped Pranav home. Over breakfast he asked only, "Are you okay?" "Thank you for not yelling," Ishita said. "Now tell me, if you want to." She did.

qa.q: What did Ishita type to her father from the bathroom?
qa.a: She typed: "Papa, please come. Sending location."

qa.q: Why did Ishita hesitate on Monday, and what changed on Saturday?
qa.a: She wasn't sure her father really meant it, but when her heart hammered at the party the offer suddenly felt worth using.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Ishita to use her father's offer?
qa.a: Safety comes first and talking later, so calling Papa got her and Pranav out without a fight.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when he saw her message?
qa.a: Papa probably felt worried but glad she trusted him, and showed it by staying calm and asking only whether she was okay.

grounding: Shows a teen using a parent's no-questions-that-night offer to get out of an unsafe party, safety first and talk later.

passage:
On the tram home in Gothenburg, Hiroshi kept replaying the party: one pull on a friend's vape, and a smirk from the others. Nothing had happened except a dizzy laugh, and yet his stomach felt like wet cement. He told himself he was a fraud. He played in the school football team, and his father coached the under-tens.
At home he skipped dinner. Astrid, a friend from school, found him on the stairwell and listened. "One time doesn't make you a bad person," she said.
"I feel horrible."
"Then tell someone who can help."
The next day he told his mum. She thanked him for being honest and asked what limits he wanted. "Not again," he said, "and I leave if it gets passed round."

qa.q: What did Hiroshi's father coach?
qa.a: Hiroshi's father coached the under-tens.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi's stomach feel like wet cement?
qa.a: He felt guilty and like a fraud, because he plays football and his father coaches, over something he had done only once.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do to set clear limits?
qa.a: He told his mum honestly and decided not to do it again and to leave if it gets passed round.

qa.q: How might Astrid see Hiroshi's mistake?
qa.a: Astrid sees a friend who made one mistake, tells him it doesn't make him a bad person and encourages him to tell someone.

grounding: Shows a teen who tried something once feeling guilty, being honest with a trusted adult and setting limits.

passage:
Monday: In the corridor, two classmates made a joke about Sharmila's skin, loud enough for the whole row to hear. Her cheeks burned and she looked at the floor.
Wednesday: The joke came back with a new nickname. This time she took a breath, said nothing, and walked to Minakshi's bench. She didn't laugh along and she didn't snap; there was nothing for them to feed on. They lost interest by lunch.
The next Tuesday: When it happened again, she had written down the dates, and she took them to the class teacher, who spoke to the two students. Minakshi sat with her in the canteen. Sharmila thought, nobody else gets a vote on what I'm worth.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do with the dates she had written down?
qa.a: She took them to the class teacher.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling in the corridor, and how do you know?
qa.a: Her cheeks burned and she looked at the floor, which shows embarrassment and hurt.

qa.q: Why did ignoring the joke, and later reporting it, work?
qa.a: Not reacting gave them nothing to feed on, and when it happened again, the written dates let a teacher step in.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's company have mattered to Sharmila?
qa.a: Sitting with her in the canteen and offering a bench to walk to told Sharmila she belonged and wasn't alone.

grounding: Shows a teen mocked about her skin, ignoring it, recording dates, telling a teacher, and keeping her worth her own.
